clue.text: Openly gay? A hindrance – escape

blocks.note: someone openly gay is out
a let is an obstruction, as in 'without let or hindrance'

explanation.surface: A gay man finding being out is a burden and wanting to flee.
explanation.walkthrough: LET as a hindrance survives in tennis and the legal phrase 'without let or hindrance'.
explanation.definitionFit: An outlet is a way out or a release, for water or feelings, so it is a means of escape.

clue.text: Mabel pissed with the drink, like mummy

indicators.note: pissed is British slang for drunk, and a drunk's letters stagger out of place

blocks.note: taken as written
the drink is slang for the sea, here the Mediterranean, the Med

explanation.surface: A drunken woman called Mabel, behaving just like her mother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The drink' is old slang for the sea. 'Mummy' looks like mother but is an Egyptian mummy.
explanation.definitionFit: Egyptian mummies were preserved with resins and spices, so being embalmed is the defining state of a mummy.

clue.text: * Ideal venue for a family row? [A BLOKE, A GENT]

definitions.text: Ideal venue for a family row?
definitions.note: defines BOATING LAKE; the entry is a punning respelling of it built on a name

indicators.note: the star marks one of the puzzle's themed clues, whose bracketed letters must be rearranged to make the entry

blocks.note: every letter in the brackets is used

explanation.surface: Where families might fall out, with a man described as both ordinary and refined.
explanation.walkthrough: A row here is a turn at the oars, not a quarrel. The entry respells boating lake with Boateng, the tailor Ozwald Boateng or the footballer brothers.
explanation.definitionFit: A boating lake is a park pond with rowing boats for hire, a natural place for a family to go rowing.

clue.text: No arse is profound

blocks.note: arse is British slang for the bottom
less means without, as in the suffix

explanation.surface: A crude saying that lacking a backside counts as deep wisdom.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in the reverse order of the clue: 'No arse' gives arse-less, read as the second piece after the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bottomless has no floor and is immeasurably deep, which is the literal sense of profound.

clue.text: Apprentice mentioned possessing "attraction"

indicators.note: to possess is to hold, so the letters sit inside the words before

blocks.note: the letters run from inside the first word into the second

explanation.surface: A trainee was said to have a certain magnetism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mentioned' looks like a sound-alike signal, but it simply hosts the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An enticement is a lure or temptation, something that draws you in, as an attraction does.

clue.text: * Anaesthetic [A VAN OK, KEN?]

definitions.note: defines NOVOCAINE; the entry is a punning respelling of it built on two surnames

indicators.note: the star marks one of the puzzle's themed clues, whose bracketed letters must be rearranged to make the entry

blocks.note: every letter in the brackets is used

explanation.surface: A painkiller, followed by a question to Ken about whether a van will do.
explanation.walkthrough: Novocaine is a dental local anaesthetic; the entry respells it as Novak (Djokovic or Kim Novak) plus Kane (the footballer Harry Kane).
explanation.definitionFit: Novocaine is a brand of procaine, a local drug that numbs pain, so it is an example of an anaesthetic.

clue.text: As an office worker casually bonked US Democrat?

indicators.note: casually means carelessly, so the letters are put down in no set order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
D is the abbreviation for Democrat

explanation.surface: An office affair with an American politician, as with Clinton and Lewinsky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bonked' is British slang for had sex with.
explanation.definitionFit: Deskbound means stuck at a desk doing office work, so it describes the state of an office worker.

clue.text: Crucial managerial group – its members get depressed

blocks.note: key means vital, crucial
a company's board manages it

explanation.surface: A vital management team whose members are all gloomy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Members get depressed' sounds like low morale, but the members are keys and depressed means pressed down.
explanation.definitionFit: A keyboard is a set of keys, and each key goes down when pressed, so its members are depressed.

clue.text: One isn't about to cut ex-PM's chief support

indicators.note: about can mean in a muddle, so the letters are rearranged
to cut into something is to go inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: a means one
taken as written
Theresa May was Prime Minister from 2016 to 2019

explanation.surface: Someone who refuses to undermine Theresa May's main ally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Isn't about to' reads as refusing to, but 'about' rearranges the letters and 'to cut' puts them inside May.
explanation.definitionFit: A mainstay is the chief rope supporting a ship's mast, so figuratively it is the principal support of anything.

clue.text: It is odd, welcoming old politician's comeback – "capital!"

indicators.note: odd means strange and irregular, so the letters are put out of order
to welcome someone is to take them in, so one piece goes inside another
a comeback is a coming back, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: taken as written
Lib is short for Liberal, the old party that became the Liberal Democrats

explanation.surface: A strange sight: a forgotten politician staging a return, greeted with cries of 'splendid!'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital!' looks like an old-fashioned cheer of approval, but it means a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Tbilisi is the capital city of Georgia, so it is an example of a capital.

clue.text: Issue a policy to get European Commission on board? That's rather uncertain

indicators.note: something on board a ship is inside it, so one piece is carried within another

blocks.note: an insurer issues a policy
EC is the abbreviation

explanation.surface: Whether to take out a policy to win over Brussels: a doubtful prospect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On board' looks like agreement, as in getting someone on side, but it means taken aboard the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Insecure means not firmly fixed or not safe, close to uncertain in the sense of unstable or doubtful.

clue.text: Sarah Palin starts changing Yale – daughter turned out

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, so only the openings are kept
changing means altering, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the first letters of the two names
taken as written
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: Sarah Palin transforms an Ivy League college, and her daughter proves a disappointment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned out' looks like 'proved to be', but it means spread outward.
explanation.definitionFit: Splayed means spread or turned outward, as feet or legs angled away from each other.

clue.text: * Prepare to sail off [I AWAKEN]

definitions.note: defines WEIGH ANCHOR; the entry is a punning respelling of it built on names

indicators.note: the star marks one of the puzzle's themed clues, whose bracketed letters must be rearranged to make the entry

blocks.note: every letter in the brackets is used

explanation.surface: A sailor getting ready to leave port at first light, waking up.
explanation.walkthrough: Weigh anchor is respelt as Wei, a Chinese name, plus Anka, as in the singer Paul Anka.
explanation.definitionFit: To weigh anchor is to raise it from the seabed, the last step before a ship can set out.

clue.text: LibDem leader stuffs college parrot

indicators.note: the leader goes first, so only the opening letter is taken
to stuff something is to fill it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: the first letter
a poly was a polytechnic, a British vocational college

explanation.surface: The Liberal Democrat leader crams a college with a talking bird.
explanation.walkthrough: Polytechnics, called polys, were British colleges until 1992.
explanation.definitionFit: Polly is the traditional name for a pet parrot, as in 'Polly wants a cracker'.

clue.text: Room freshener locates focus of stink in cruddy tavern

indicators.note: the focus is the centre, so only the middle letter is taken
to locate something in a place is to put it there, so one piece goes inside another
cruddy means dirty and messy, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: the middle letter of the five
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something to freshen a grubby pub finds where the smell is coming from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Room freshener' looks like an aerosol spray, but it is the opening that lets fresh air in.
explanation.definitionFit: An air vent is an opening that lets air circulate, so it freshens a room.

clue.text: * Infantile joke item [IS NO HIGH-UP COW]

definitions.note: defines WHOOPEE CUSHION; the entry is a punning respelling of it built on two names

indicators.note: the star marks one of the puzzle's themed clues, whose bracketed letters must be rearranged to make the entry

blocks.note: every letter in the brackets is used

explanation.surface: A childish prank, with a dismissive remark about some woman not being important.
explanation.walkthrough: A whoopee cushion makes a rude noise when sat on; the entry respells it as Whoopi Goldberg plus Peter Cushing, the horror actor.
explanation.definitionFit: A whoopee cushion is a rubber bag that makes a fart noise, a stock example of a childish practical joke.

clue.text: An element of internet shag: having skinny toes

blocks.note: the World Wide Web is one part of the internet
to bed someone is to have sex with them, and shag is British slang for the same

explanation.surface: Online sex, described with an odd remark about thin toes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skinny toes' looks like thin toes, but means toes joined by skin, like a duck's.
explanation.definitionFit: Webbed feet have skin stretched between the toes, so they are toes with skin, skinny in a punning sense.

clue.text: Liberal Party's dough

indicators.note: liberal means free and unrestricted, so the letters are allowed to move

blocks.note: taken as written, dropping the apostrophe

explanation.surface: The Liberal Party's money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal Party' looks like one name, and 'dough' like money, but each word has its own job.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastry is a dough of flour, fat and water used for pies and tarts.

clue.text: 'Vicar' uselessly protecting failed high flier

indicators.note: to protect is to shield and hold close, so the letters sit inside the words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A man posing as a vicar who fails to shield a disgraced high achiever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High flier' reads as a successful person, but here it is meant literally.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Icarus flew too near the sun on wax wings, which melted, so he fell to his death.

clue.text: Hold member by hair

blocks.note: an arm is a limb, or member
a lock is a tress of hair

explanation.surface: Grabbing someone, or a club member, by their hair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' looks like a club member, but it is the old word for a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: An armlock is a wrestling grip that pins an opponent's arm, a kind of hold.

clue.text: see 1d.
* Complete rubbish [BOLD, ALL EARS]

definitions.note: defines LOAD OF BALLS; the entry is a punning respelling of it built on a name

indicators.note: the star marks one of the puzzle's themed clues, whose bracketed letters must be rearranged to make the entry

blocks.note: every letter in the brackets is used

explanation.surface: Total nonsense, set beside someone brave and listening intently.
explanation.walkthrough: Load of balls is British slang for nonsense; said quickly it sounds like LOADER BALLS, bringing in the Labour politician Ed Balls.
explanation.definitionFit: A load of balls is a vulgar British idiom for nonsense, so it matches total drivel or garbage.

clue.text: Gove? Claim he's pathetic

indicators.note: pathetic means feeble and in a sorry state, so the letters collapse into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, dropping the apostrophe-s

explanation.surface: A jibe at the Conservative minister: he is said to be feeble.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark shows that Gove is an example: Michael Gove, the Conservative cabinet minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael is the first name of the politician Michael Gove, so the surname clues his forename.

clue.text: Female screw locks up daughter

indicators.note: to lock up is to shut inside, so one piece is held within another

blocks.note: lay and screw are both slang for having sex
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A woman prison officer who imprisons a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screw' is British slang for a prison guard, which the surface uses, but here it is the vulgar verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady is a polite term for a woman, so it works as a noun for a female.

clue.text: Prue powerless with canned bananas' stickability

indicators.note: less power means the abbreviation for power is removed from the word
bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild

blocks.note: the name losing P, for power
taken as written

explanation.surface: Prue Leith, the TV cookery judge, grimly persisting with tinned fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' looks like the tinned fruit, but it is the slang for mad and signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Stickability is informal for the ability to persist, the same quality as staying power or endurance.

clue.text: Ivanka is, er, sh*t, hosting rulers

indicators.note: a host has guests inside, so the letters lie within the words

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word across the next two into the last

explanation.surface: A stammering verdict that Ivanka Trump is useless, at a gathering of world leaders.
explanation.walkthrough: The asterisk in 'sh*t' is ignored; only the letters before it count.
explanation.definitionFit: Kaiser was the title of the German and Austrian emperors, so kaisers are imperial rulers.

clue.text: Cheap car which an evasive politician will give you

definitions.text: which an evasive politician will give you

blocks.note: first meaning: a small, inexpensive car for local trips

blocks.clueFragment: which an evasive politician will give you
blocks.note: second meaning: evasive treatment

explanation.walkthrough: A runaround is British for a small, cheap car used for short trips. To give someone the runaround is to dodge them.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun covers both a budget car for errands and the deceptive evasion that politicians dish out in interviews.
